title: Notes from First Contact: Learning to Code
summary: Looking back on my first programming job — and how I learned to write code in the first place.
markdown:
Looking back on my first programming job, I want to start with how I learned to code at all.

## College

I was a networking major. Sophomore year I joined a programming training class run by a teacher — miss the bar and you were out. At the time I could write exactly one line:

```plain text
System.out.println("Hello World");
```

Early on, the goal was just survive the assigned problems and not get cut. I leaned on Baidu hard, without understanding a single line.

Midway through, we had to stand up and explain what every line did. Pasting code wasn't enough anymore. I started looking up each statement — English-to-Chinese, basically. Somehow I made it through.

Later the problems got harder. One of them was a hand-written calculator that had to respect the rules of `+ - * /`. That problem is what actually got me in. I finally felt the core of programming: if you can think it through, the machine can do it.

## Internship

My teacher recommended me into a company placement at State Grid. After work I'd go home and study — MongoDB, VMs, Hadoop, whatever. I didn't understand most of it, but I walked every tutorial end to end. I still remember spinning up several VMs on my laptop just to stand up Hadoop, following the docs step by step, and the pure lift when it finally worked.

Later the same teacher pointed me at JavaScript. Then jQuery. That was the door into frontend.

## First programming job

I joined as a frontend engineer. The stack was still template languages — slow to ship. On a new project I pushed for a frontend/backend split. I also built a jQuery helper that could spin up lists and forms fast: backend only needed to expose the API and fields; I'd write JSON in a config file and have a module ready in minutes. The backend guys were genuinely shocked.

That's when the frontend career really started.

## Closing

There's no shortcut. You grind, and you put in the hours. My teacher used to say: among the people in that training class, I wasn't the smartest — I was the most stubborn. Most of this path was time, spent deliberately. That time bought me a few real skills:

- Search — knowing how to look things up cuts the time-to-answer dramatically
- Learning — picking up tech I'd never touched before without freezing
- Flexibility — switching across languages without needing a long runway
sourceTitle: 我的编程启示录：第一次敲代码的感悟
